A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for the first 15 cycles, the PN waveforms are accurate, but for the last 15, the PN approximants are inaccurate, but the TaylorT4 approximant is accurate.

, in the last 15 orbits before merger, the 3.5 post-Newtonian phase and 3.0 PN amplitude approximants agree very well with numerical simulations, but generic post-Newtonian formulae at 3.0 and 3.5 PN order do not.
the numerical and post-Newtonial waveforms agree well over the first ~10 cycles, and that TaylorT4 at the 3.5 post-Newtonian approximation agrees well over the first 30 cycles.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the PN waveform approximants that have become standard in the gravitational-wave data analysis community are not sufficiently accurate to match numerical waveforms in the last 15 orbits before merger.

PN theory can be used to predict numerical results with high confidence in the early inspiral, but that caution is required in the late inspiral, especially when using TaylorT4 at the 3.0–3.5PN level, which may have some residual systematic errors.

, for the first time, we are able to use PN theory to make accurate predictions of the gravitational waveform of a coalescing black hole binary system, and we are able to compare numerical relativity simulations of black-hole binary systems with PN theory.
